name: MCP Database Servers
title: MCP Database Servers
answer: Model Context Protocol servers expose a database to an AI assistant as a set of tools, such as listing tables, describing a schema and running a query. This site's MCP directory tracks active servers, including many for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and cloud warehouses. The directory currently lists 2511 active MCP servers, of which 263 are for SQL databases and warehouses. That makes database access one of the larger single purposes a server is built for.

sections.body: Model Context Protocol servers expose a database to an AI assistant as a set of tools, such as listing tables, describing a schema and running a query. This site's MCP directory tracks active servers, including many for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and cloud warehouses. The directory currently lists 2511 active MCP servers, of which 263 are for SQL databases and warehouses. That makes database access one of the larger single purposes a server is built for.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A database server runs either as a local process on the analyst's machine or as a remote service, and it speaks JSON-RPC over standard input and output or over HTTP. It holds a connection to the database through the vendor's driver, for example psycopg for PostgreSQL, and reads its credentials from environment variables or a configuration file supplied by the assistant host. Some teams run the server in a container next to the database, others keep it on the workstation. This site's own pages are built from a PostgreSQL database, the same kind of source these servers are pointed at.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The server publishes a small set of tools, typically listing tables, describing a table and running a query. The assistant chooses a tool, fills in the arguments, and the server executes the call and returns rows as text or JSON. Many servers restrict execution to SELECT statements or apply a row limit, and some cache the schema so the model does not rediscover tables on every turn. Write access, where a server offers it, is usually a separate tool that is disabled by default.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are credentials that are broader than the task needs, prompt injection through data the model reads, and queries that scan or lock more than intended. Provenance matters because a result the assistant reports may come from a query the user never saw, so servers that log the SQL they run make review easier. In practice, access follows the database's own roles, with a read-only account for exploration and a narrower grant for anything that writes. The server's own license and maintenance record vary by project, so the repository is the place to check them.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Growth in the directory points to more servers for warehouses and analytical engines, not only transactional databases. Closer integration with schema metadata is likely, so a server can hand the model column descriptions and relationships rather than bare table names. Query review and audit logging are moving into the server itself, since that is the point where the SQL is visible. Common tool names and result shapes would let an assistant move between servers without relearning each one.
